find: Ferrous metals are magnetic and can rust. Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron, are not magnetic, and generally do not rust in the same way. A simple magnetism test can separate the two families.
replace: Ferrous metals often rust. Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron and generally do not rust in the same way. Magnetism alone cannot separate the two families.
note: F1: Magnetism does not reliably distinguish ferrous from non-ferrous metals.

find: • Ferrous metals contain iron and are typically magnetic; non-ferrous metals do not contain iron and are not magnetic. Ferrous metals rust; non-ferrous metals generally do not.
replace: • Ferrous metals contain iron; non-ferrous metals do not. Magnetism alone cannot identify a metal family. Ferrous metals can rust; non-ferrous metals generally do not.
note: F1: Retain iron content as the classification rule.

expect: Yes — ferrous metals are typically magnetic; non-ferrous metals are not.
value: Not always. Many ferrous metals are magnetic, but magnetism alone cannot identify a metal family.
note: F1: The answer must not treat magnetism as a reliable classification test.

expect: Any thermoplastic that softens on heating — acrylic is the most common spec example.
note: F2: Supply all three thermoplastics named in the specification.

find: • Thermoplastics (acrylic, nylon, HIPS) can be recycled — polymer chains re-soften on heating. Thermosetting plastics (urea formaldehyde, silicone) cannot — cross-linked structure is permanent.
replace: • Thermoplastics (acrylic, nylon, HIPS) can be re-shaped by heating. Thermosetting plastics (urea formaldehyde, silicone) cannot be re-melted after curing because their cross-linked structure is permanent.
note: F3: State the settled re-melting distinction without claiming all recycling is impossible.

find: Thermosetting plastics cannot be recycled because heating does not re-soften them — their cross-linked bonds are permanent.
replace: Thermosetting plastics cannot be re-melted after curing because heating does not re-soften them — their cross-linked bonds are permanent.
note: F3: Recycling is broader than re-melting.

expect: Plastics that are permanently hardened during curing through cross-linking of polymer chains, and cannot be re-melted or recycled — examples include urea formaldehyde and silicone.
value: Plastics that harden during curing through cross-linking of polymer chains and cannot be re-melted after curing — examples include urea formaldehyde and silicone.
note: F3: Keep the definition technically accurate.

find: The ten physical properties are: tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, corrosion resistance and elasticity.
replace: The ten physical properties are: tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, conductivity, corrosion resistance, environmental degradation and elasticity.
note: F4: Use the specification’s ten-property list.

find: The ten physical properties — tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, corrosion resistance and elasticity — are distinct. Never use them as synonyms.
replace: The ten physical properties — tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, conductivity, corrosion resistance, environmental degradation and elasticity — are distinct. Never use them as synonyms.
note: F4: Restore environmental degradation to the specification list.

find: Using Ohm’s law (V = IR), the resistance can be calculated, which is the inverse of conductivity.
replace: Using Ohm’s law (V = IR), the resistance can be calculated. With the sample’s dimensions, this gives resistivity; conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity.
note: F5: Resistance depends on sample geometry.
F6: The specification does not classify hardness testing as destructive.

find: Although the indenter leaves a mark in the surface, the sample is generally not destroyed, so hardness testing is sometimes described as semi-destructive. For exam purposes, the specification lists it under destructive testing, so classify it accordingly.
replace: The indenter leaves a mark in the surface. Whether that makes the test unsuitable depends on whether the component can still be used after marking.
note: F6: Remove the unsupported specification classification.

find: Destructive Tests for Malleability, Ductility and Elasticity
replace: Tests for Malleability, Ductility and Elasticity
note: F6: Some of these tests can be non-destructive when the component remains usable.

find: • Destructive testing (tensile test, impact test, hardness test) permanently damages or destroys the sample but gives precise measurements of properties such as tensile strength, toughness and hardness.
replace: • Destructive testing, such as tensile and impact testing, permanently damages or destroys the sample and gives measurements of properties such as tensile strength and toughness.
note: F6: Do not state that the specification places hardness testing under destructive testing.

expect: A hardness test leaves an indent but the sample is not fractured. Why is it still classified as destructive in the specification?
value: What limitation can a hardness-test indent create for a finished component?
note: F6: The original question makes an unsupported specification claim.

expect: Because it permanently marks the sample surface, so it is listed under destructive testing.
value: It leaves a permanent indent, so it may be unsuitable for a finished component.
note: F6: Preserve the practical limitation without an unsupported classification.

value: The specification names three thermoplastics: acrylic, nylon and which polystyrene grade?
